doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

chapter: Billy Taylor years and the greats
title: Looking back on the great bands and his changing sense of time
summary: May was scared when playing with greats; now struggles with the beat and discusses it with Charles McPherson.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: In retrospect, when you think about playing with Coltrane and Miles and Charlie Parker, is there things that stick out in you mind that maybe at the time didn’t make an impression on you but in later years? That’s an awful big question.

It is. Let’s see if I can break it down. I hope I can answer your question. You know when you’re going through these things, let’s say, what I get from your question is when you’re going through these things it’s not like another gig because I was scared to death. I was really scared. But when you look back now, or even I can really see the magnitude, if there is such a word, of what I had done, you know being in those bands and playing with those great, great people. I mean if I could have done that now, I just wish I could, you know, what I know now, even though I felt, and Charles McPherson and I talk about this quite a bit. And it seems that the older you get you don’t really have — you lose some things and you gain some things. So you have the knowledge but for some reason or another I’m having more trouble now with the beat. You know when I was younger, I can hear some of the recordings I made and it was very, very natural for me to stand up there and just never, I mean my time was just like a metronome. I mean that’s one of the nice things I could say about myself. I had really good time. I was probably noted for that. But now it seems to me I’m having so much trouble just trying to keep that thing steady. And I can’t figure out what it is.
I mean playing the bass is pretty physical.

It is. Yeah it is. But I really can’t figure out what it is. Charles McPherson and I talk about it like I said before. But he thinks that, you know I’m not mentioning any names, but when you start listening to people that are around my age, we listen to records that they made thirty years ago, forty years ago, and the way they play now, and you play with them live, it’s a little different. Everybody seems to not be in the pocket like as easily as it used to be.
